summary:
Ontario stands under the national framework of Canada; this assessment covers Ontario's own layer: its human rights code, the commission that administers it, the province's published policy, and Ontario's recorded hate-crime figures.

The Ontario Human Rights Commission's policy on gender identity and gender expression states that under the Ontario Human Rights Code people are protected from discrimination and harassment on those grounds in employment, housing, facilities and services, contracts, and membership in unions, trade or professional associations. The policy defines gender identity as a person's internal and individual experience of gender and notes that a chosen name and pronoun are common ways of expressing gender. It is the official provincial statement of the human-rights protections a trans person holds in Ontario's workplaces, housing and services.

Statistics Canada reported on 30 March 2026 that police recorded 4,882 hate crimes in Canada in 2024, 1% more than in 2023, at a national rate of 12.1 per 100,000. Ontario recorded the highest provincial rate at 16.0 incidents per 100,000 population. The figure covers all reported motivations and does not isolate gender-identity motivation. Police figures capture only reported incidents, and reporting levels are shaped by awareness and community trust.

On 28 August 2023 Ontario education minister Stephen Lecce said parents 'must be fully involved and fully aware' of a child's decision to use a different name or pronoun at school. He said teachers and school boards already weigh 'exceptional circumstances' and potential harm to the child. Ontario had not adopted parental-consent legislation of the kind other provinces were enacting at that time, and no later Ontario legislative instance on this question is documented in this record.
tangentialFactors:
The education minister's August 2023 remarks were made amid legislative activity on student name and pronoun changes in other Canadian provinces; the contrast matters for a visitor with school-age children, because Ontario's position at that date rested on ministerial direction and school-board practice rather than statute.

Ontario's 16.0 incidents per 100,000 for 2024 is a per-capita rate, so the province's first-place ranking among Canadian provinces is not a population artefact. It measures police-reported hate crime of all motivations combined and therefore indicates the provincial reporting and enforcement environment a trans visitor would enter, not a trans-specific rate.
localsOnly:
Residents discriminated against on gender identity or gender expression grounds in Ontario raise complaints under the Ontario Human Rights Code, which the Ontario Human Rights Commission administers and whose protections the commission sets out in its published policy on gender identity and gender expression.

For families, the documented provincial position as of 28 August 2023 is that parents are to be fully involved and fully aware when a student decides to use a different name or pronoun at school, with teachers and school boards directed to weigh exceptional circumstances and potential harm to the child.
blindOutOfScope:
No trans-specific killing or violent incident in the state/province is documented in this inventory, and no trans-specific figure with a stated period is available, so no trans-specific rate can be stated for the state/province.

The 2024 hate-crime figure covers all reported motivations and does not break out gender-identity motivation for the state/province. A national LGBTIQ+ organisation's analysis of 2024 police-reported data covering sexual-orientation and gender-identity motivations exists but is national in scope and is not broken down to the state/province here.

Whether the state/province legislated parental consent for student name or pronoun changes after the 28 August 2023 statement is unresolved in this record; the most recent dated item on that question is 28 August 2023, and no later instance is documented.

No state/province-specific public-opinion survey on acceptance of transgender people is sourced here, so no local prevalence figure for attitudes can be given.
